items.body: The quality of what AI produces depends heavily on the quality of what you ask it — treat prompt engineering as a genuine skill, not an afterthought.

items.lead: Stay a continuous learner as the tools keep changing.
items.body: Build real AI literacy — how algorithms work at a working level, and what their ethical implications actually are — rather than treating today's version as the finished article.

items.lead: Sharpen the skills machines can't do.
items.body: As AI absorbs more routine work, prioritise critical thinking, creativity, complex communication, emotional intelligence and interdisciplinary collaboration — the capabilities that become more valuable, not less.

items.lead: Treat feedback as training, not just correction.
items.body: Give AI tools clear, constructive feedback to refine their output for your specific context — a diligent, literal assistant improves with direction, not silence.

items.lead: Mind what you actually feed into the system.
items.body: Be deliberate about data privacy and security, especially with cloud-based tools — know how your input is used and stored before you share it.

items.lead: Assume bias is present until you've checked.
items.body: AI models inherit and can amplify the biases in their training data — critically evaluate outputs for fairness and accuracy, especially in sensitive contexts.

items.lead: Say plainly when AI did the work.
items.body: Be transparent about AI's role in anything that might be read as human-made, and stay alert to the wider societal impact of adopting it — in your field and beyond.

note: A radiologist reviewing a stack of scans notices they've started agreeing with the AI's flag before they've finished looking at the image themselves. Not because they checked and it matched — because it's been right the last dozen times, and matching is faster than looking. They catch themselves mid-glance on scan thirteen and force themselves to look again, properly. It's clean. The AI was right. They still don't know, in that moment, whether they looked or whether they trusted.

This is happening in offices, hospitals, courtrooms and classrooms — wherever a system offers a recommendation fast enough to arrive before the person has finished forming their own view. None of it is malicious, and most of it looks like good practice: using the tool for what it's good at. The risk isn't that AI takes over. It's that the habit of checking quietly erodes, one correct answer at a time, until nobody notices when it stops being checked at all.

The card holds four practice areas across two columns: knowing precisely where AI's strengths and limits actually sit, integrating tools deliberately rather than by default, building the collaborative skills and literacy that keep pace with the tools, and staying honest about privacy, bias and disclosure as the relationship deepens. Written for anyone who has caught themselves trusting an AI's output before they'd finished forming their own.
It comes from The Next Evolution, where the fuller argument lives. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, or send it to whoever just told you AI "basically decided" something and seemed relieved about it.
So next time a system hands you an answer before you've finished thinking it through: did you decide, or did you just agree?

understanding-your-cognitive-limits.title: Understanding Your Cognitive Limits
understanding-your-cognitive-limits.line: For the moment you realise you’ve read the same paragraph three times and none of it landed.
understanding-your-cognitive-limits.subtitle: Attention is a finite resource, and your brain has built-in limitations. This pause turns that theory into a practical awareness of where your focus actually goes.
understanding-your-cognitive-limits.quote: The future will be shaped by what we choose to attend to.

items.lead: Notice when you're most focused during the day, and protect that window for your hardest work.
items.body: Schedule demanding tasks for the hours your mind is naturally sharpest, not whenever they happen to land on the calendar.

items.lead: Build a dedicated space for deep work, free of notifications and background noise.
items.body: A focus zone you enter deliberately, not one you hope to find amid the usual pings and digital temptations.

items.lead: Choose one task and stay with it, even for short stretches.
items.body: Every switch between tasks carries a hidden cost — single-tasking rebuilds the muscle that constant switching wears down.

items.lead: Treat sleep as a non-negotiable part of your routine, not the first thing you cut.
items.body: Adequate sleep is a critical input to focus and mental clarity — not a reward for finishing everything else.

items.lead: Break complex information into smaller pieces before you try to hold it all in mind.
items.body: Short-term memory has a real limit — respecting it prevents the overload that stalls thinking altogether.

items.lead: Studies selective, sustained and divided attention.
items.body: Including phenomena like inattentional blindness and change blindness.

items.lead: Researches the brain regions and neural networks behind attention.
items.body: Covering how focus is directed, maintained and shifted.

items.lead: Studies the limits of short-term memory, such as Miller's "Magic Number".
items.body: And what those limits mean for how information actually gets processed.

items.lead: Examines how sleep deprivation and sleep quality affect the mind.
items.body: Attention, memory, decision-making and overall cognitive performance are all at stake.

items.lead: Looks at whether mindfulness and meditation actually improve focus.
items.body: Alongside other cognitive training techniques aimed at reducing distractibility.

closing.lead: This isn't about achieving perfect focus overnight.
closing.body: It's about shifting from passive reaction to active observation. Your chaotic attention isn't a personal failing — it's a predictable consequence of your brain and the modern world. Building awareness reclaims agency and lays the groundwork for a more intentional life.

note: You've read the same paragraph three times and still can't repeat it back. Not because the material is hard — because your attention left the page ten minutes ago and your eyes kept moving without it. It happens by mid-afternoon, in the middle of the one email that actually mattered, on the fourth hour of a task that needed maybe ninety minutes of real focus.

That's not a discipline problem. Attention is a finite resource, and the brain that keeps drifting has real, built-in limits — not a character flaw showing itself. The card's own framing is plain about this: it isn't about achieving perfect focus overnight, it's about turning that theory into a practical awareness of where your attention is actually going.

The card holds ten prompts across two columns. Five habits to try this week — finding your natural attention peak and protecting it, building a space genuinely free of distraction, practising single tasks instead of switching between them, treating sleep as non-negotiable, and breaking complex information down before it overwhelms you. And five fields of research if you want the science behind the pull, from the real limits of working memory to what sleep deprivation actually costs your thinking.
It comes from The Cognitive Crucible, where the fuller argument about attention as a finite, contested resource plays out. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, or pin it somewhere you'll see it before the next task that needs your full attention.
So next time you catch yourself rereading the same line: is the material actually hard, or did your attention leave the room a while ago?

practise-the-three-foot-world-in-a-digit.title: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
practise-the-three-foot-world-in-a-digit.line: For the evening you’ve read about four crises on three continents and haven’t spoken to anyone in the house.
practise-the-three-foot-world-in-a-digit.subtitle: The feed invites you to live everywhere at once, while the only ground you can actually change stays within arm's reach.
practise-the-three-foot-world-in-a-digit.quote: The greatest technology of all is still us.

items.lead: Notice what actually pulls your focus away from the present.
items.body: Turn off the notifications that don't earn their interruption, and make using technology something you choose deliberately rather than something you fall into.

items.lead: Define the radius of action you can genuinely affect this week.
items.body: The tasks, conversations and relationships that sit within your sphere of influence — and, by naming them, the ones that sit outside it.

items.lead: Put your time into the people you can actually reach.
items.body: Face-to-face, local and tangible interaction is where your presence changes something; be present where your presence matters.

items.lead: When overwhelm hits, ask what you can touch, change or improve within the next three feet.
items.body: The question converts a general sense of helplessness into one specific action available to you today.

groups.heading: Reclaim the Rituals of the Physical

items.lead: Write with a pen. Walk without headphones. Speak without a screen between you.
items.body: Cognitive depth rebuilds through sensory simplicity, not through a better-designed app.

items.lead: Build services that keep a person within reach of the decision.
items.body: Physical presence, emotional proximity or localised decision-making each keep a service answerable to someone who can see its effect.

items.lead: Push power and resources out to the frontline.
items.body: Schools, clinics, libraries and neighbourhood groups already know what their community needs; autonomy is what lets them act on it.

groups.heading: Reduce Cognitive Load in Service Design

items.lead: Simplify forms, processes and interfaces until anxiety stops being part of the transaction.
items.body: People should be able to understand and complete what you ask of them without needing help to do it.

items.lead: Reward the initiatives that change something in the community this quarter.
items.body: Immediate local effect is a harder measure to report than an abstract KPI, and a more honest one.

items.lead: Test policies and technologies in specific communities before you scale them.
items.body: The three-foot world is where real feedback lives; a pilot that never touches one tells you very little.

note: Someone puts their phone down at ten past eleven. In the previous forty minutes they have read about a war, a flood, a funding scandal and a company going under. They know a great deal more than they did at half past ten, and they can act on precisely none of it. In the same forty minutes, the person in the next room went to bed without being spoken to.

Scale is what's doing the damage here. The feed hands you the whole world at once and invites you to care about all of it equally, which in practice means caring about none of it particularly. Agency stays stubbornly local. It sits in the room you're in, the street you're on, the conversation you could have tomorrow morning — and none of that competes well for attention against a continent on fire.

The card holds ten practices across two columns. Five for individuals: auditing what actually pulls your focus, drawing a weekly radius of action, anchoring in the relationships you can reach, asking what you can touch or change within the next three feet when overwhelm hits, and returning to the physical rituals that rebuild cognitive depth. Five for organisations and leaders, which turn out to be the same principle at institutional scale — design for proximity, push autonomy to the frontline, cut the cognitive load out of your services, reward local effect over abstract measures, and prototype where real feedback lives.
It comes from The Next Evolution, where the fuller argument sits. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, or pin it somewhere you'll see it on the evening you've read too much and done nothing.
So next time you surface from a long scroll through other people's emergencies: what did you learn, and what could you actually do about any of it?

asserting-your-data-rights.title: Asserting Your Data Rights
asserting-your-data-rights.line: For the moment you click “Accept All” without reading past the first line, and want to change that.
asserting-your-data-rights.subtitle: Your data rights are only real if you use them. This pause turns the fine print you usually skip into leverage you can actually act on.
asserting-your-data-rights.quote: The future will be shaped by what we choose to attend to.

items.lead: Search each privacy policy for two questions: what data do they collect, and how do they use it.
items.body: Skip the legal boilerplate around them — those two sections carry almost everything you actually need to know.

items.lead: Use the data access and deletion rights a service actually offers you.
items.body: A right sitting unused in a settings menu protects nobody — request your data, or ask for it to be deleted.

items.lead: Try a browser or extension built to limit what gets tracked about you.
items.body: Small switches, a different browser, a tracker blocker, change how much of your activity gets collected by default.

items.lead: Support the companies that make their privacy controls clear and easy to use.
items.body: Where you spend your attention and your custom is itself a signal platforms read and respond to.

items.lead: Read consent requests instead of clicking straight through them.
items.body: Choose the granular option where one exists, rather than accepting the broadest default.

items.lead: Studies how data protection regulations get written, applied and enforced.
items.body: GDPR and CCPA are the most cited examples, but the same questions recur wherever the law tries to catch up.

items.lead: Develops cryptographic techniques and tools that limit what data has to be exposed.
items.body: The aim is data that stays useful without staying visible to everyone who touches it.

items.lead: Debates who actually owns your data, and what companies owe you because of it.
items.body: Legal and philosophical arguments about ownership, identity and the responsibilities of holding someone else's information.

items.lead: Traces how breaches happen once data has been aggregated at scale.
items.body: The bigger the collection, the bigger the target, and the more people affected when it fails.

items.lead: Studies how people's attitudes to privacy actually shape their digital habits.
items.body: The gap between what people say they want and what they click through is itself the subject.

closing.lead: This isn't about reading every privacy policy end to end.
closing.body: It's about becoming a digital citizen rather than a passive user — someone whose small, deliberate choices, and voice in the wider conversation, count as a vote for a digital world where technology serves people instead of exploiting them.

note: You've clicked "Accept All" on a cookie banner without reading it more times than you could count. Getting on with the page mattered more, in the moment, than knowing what you'd just agreed to. Somewhere in that fine print is nearly everything a company needs to know before it does what it wants with your data, and almost nobody reads far enough to find it.

That's not really a failure of attention. It's a document built long, a clause buried deep, a path of least resistance that always points towards yes. Rights exist to counter that design: to see what's held on you, to have it corrected or deleted, to ask a company what it's actually doing with what you gave it. A right nobody exercises isn't functioning as a right.

The card holds ten prompts across two columns. Five habits to try this week — reading a privacy policy for exactly two questions instead of the whole document, using the access and deletion rights already sitting in an account's settings, trying a browser or extension built to limit tracking, backing the companies that make their controls genuinely clear, and reading consent requests instead of clicking straight past them. And five fields of research if you want to go further, from the regulation behind GDPR and CCPA to the philosophy of who actually owns your data in the first place.
It comes from The Cognitive Crucible, where the fuller argument about attention and agency in a system built to erode both plays out. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, or keep it somewhere you'll see it before the next cookie banner asks for your yes.
Next time a consent form asks for thirty seconds of your attention: will you give it, or keep scrolling past, the way you always have?

design-digital-humans-with-intention.title: Design Digital Humans with Intention
design-digital-humans-with-intention.line: For when the voice on the other end of a public service turns out not to be a person, and no one thought to say so.
design-digital-humans-with-intention.subtitle: Building the AI avatars and virtual agents that now speak for public services with the accountability, consent and human escalation the people meeting them are owed.
design-digital-humans-with-intention.quote: The greatest technology of all is still us.

items.lead: Make it clear when someone is speaking to AI, not a person.
items.body: Build standards around transparency, inclusivity and consent, and give every user an easy way to escalate to a human.

items.lead: Bring community stakeholders into the room before the script is written.
items.body: Involve them in shaping a digital human's language, expressions and emotional responses, so bias in culture, race or gender doesn't get built in unnoticed.

items.lead: Test the language model and its affective computing regularly.
items.body: Look for unintended persuasion, exclusion or emotional profiling before the public finds it for you.

items.lead: Never trap a user inside a conversation with a machine.
items.body: Keep a visible, accessible route to a human on hand, especially once a case turns sensitive or complex.

items.lead: Track sentiment and stress signals through every interaction.
items.body: A digital human should ease the public's mental load, not quietly add to it.

items.lead: Insist on being told when you're talking to a non-human agent.
items.body: And demand the option to speak with a person when you need to.

items.lead: Call out a digital human when it gets something wrong.
items.body: Failing to understand you, excluding your dialect, or handling distress without any care are all worth reporting, not just tolerating.

items.lead: Push for transparency in who actually built and runs it.
items.body: Public, private or somewhere in between, accountability shouldn't be a mystery.

items.lead: Take part in the civic conversation about digital empathy in public services.
items.body: An interaction with the state should never be a black box.

note: A resident logs on to renew a blue badge, or chase a repair, and finds themselves typing to a face that nods, blinks and says "I understand you" in a voice built for reassurance. Nobody told them it was AI. There was no button marked for a person. The conversation just continued, patient and warm, until the resident gave up guessing and hung up.

Digital humans — avatars built to stand in front of the public on behalf of a service — are already live across government and healthcare settings. Every choice about how one speaks, when it escalates, and what it's permitted to notice about someone's distress was made months earlier, by people that resident will never meet. Most of those choices stay invisible until the day they fail somebody.

The card holds nine practices across two columns. Five for the public sector leaders commissioning and shaping these systems: adopting ethical design frameworks, bringing community voices in before the script is written, auditing for bias and manipulation, designing a real path to a human, and monitoring the emotional toll an interaction leaves behind. Four for the citizens and civil society groups meeting them: knowing the right to be told, reporting failures instead of shrugging them off, pushing for transparency in who actually owns the system, and staying in the civic conversation about what digital empathy is for.

It comes from The Next Evolution, where the wider argument — that technology should be built for the person in front of it, not the average user or the efficiency target it's meant to hit — is made at length. The card stands on its own.
Print it, or send it to whoever is briefing the next digital human into service.
What happens to the person who never works out they were talking to a machine at all?

navigating-the-ai-curated-world.title: Navigating the AI-Curated World
navigating-the-ai-curated-world.line: For when you can't tell whether an idea found you, or was placed in front of you.
navigating-the-ai-curated-world.subtitle: The feed decides what reaches you before you ever choose to look. This pause turns that fact into deliberate scrutiny you can actually use.
navigating-the-ai-curated-world.quote: The future will be shaped by what we choose to attend to.

items.lead: Ask where a piece of information actually came from before you believe it.
items.body: Be especially wary when it feels too perfect, too sensational, or oddly tailored to exactly what interests you.

items.lead: Check for any label or disclaimer that marks content as AI-generated or AI-assisted.
items.body: These disclosures are appearing more often — reading past them defeats the point of them existing.

items.lead: Cross-check anything that matters against more than one reputable source.
items.body: A claim that only appears in one place, however confidently stated, hasn't earned your trust yet.

items.lead: Learn to recognise the common forms AI-generated content takes.
items.body: Deepfakes and AI-written text each leave their own tells once you know what to look for.

items.lead: Talk to the people around you about what generative AI is doing to information and trust.
items.body: The conversation sharpens your own scepticism, and theirs.

items.lead: Studies the ethical questions generative AI raises, including bias, misinformation and accountability.
items.body: The questions recur wherever a system now makes a judgement call a person used to make instead.

groups.heading: Cognitive Science of Perception and Memory

items.lead: Studies how the brain processes and stores information.
items.body: And how AI-generated content might influence or manipulate that process without you noticing.

items.lead: Studies what happens to work and creativity when humans and AI create content together.
items.body: The interesting question is what each side actually contributes, not just that the two now work together.

items.lead: Traces how generative AI is used to create and spread false narratives.
items.body: And the strategies researchers and platforms are testing to combat them.

items.lead: Develops curricula and tools that help people understand and critically engage with AI technologies.
items.body: The aim is a public that can question a system's output, not just consume it.

closing.lead: This isn't about achieving perfect objectivity.
closing.body: It's about becoming an active sense-maker rather than a passive consumer of whatever the feed curates — building your own understanding through critical thinking, varied sources and conscious choice, so your beliefs stay yours rather than an algorithm's design.

note: You read something on your phone that agrees with you almost too well — the argument, the tone, even the example, sitting exactly where your own thinking already was. A year ago you'd have called that confirmation. Increasingly, it's worth asking whether it's construction.

Generative AI hasn't only changed what gets written; it's changed how much of what reaches you was ever chosen by anyone at all, human or otherwise. The feed decides before you do, and most of that deciding happens somewhere you can't see it. This pause is for the part of the process you can still get back.

The card lays out ten things to explore, in two columns. Try Something is five habits for anyone reading a feed today — questioning a source, checking for an AI disclosure, cross-verifying a claim before it settles into belief. Learn Something is five fields worth a longer look, from AI ethics and governance to the cognitive science of how perception and memory actually work, for anyone who wants the mechanism underneath the habit.
It comes from The Cognitive Crucible, where the fuller argument about cognitive agency in an AI-curated world gets made at length. The card doesn't need the book to make sense — it stands on its own.
Print it, pin it by your desk, or send it to whoever in your life still assumes their feed is neutral.
The card doesn't answer the harder question: once you know the feed is choosing for you, how much of what you already believe are you willing to go back and check?

secure-the-smart-home.title: Secure the Smart Home
secure-the-smart-home.line: For the moment you realise nobody in the house has thought about the smart speaker's security since the day it went in the box.
secure-the-smart-home.subtitle: Every device you add to your home network is another door — and most of them still use the password they arrived with.
secure-the-smart-home.quote: A smart home is only as secure as its weakest device.

sections.label: Securing the Smart Home and IoT

items.lead: Isolate your smart devices on their own network.
items.body: Create a separate, dedicated guest Wi-Fi network for every IoT device — cameras, thermostats, speakers — so a compromised device can't move laterally into your laptop, your work systems or your financial data.

items.lead: Replace every factory password before you switch a device on.
items.body: Default logins like “admin” or “123456” are the first thing an attacker tries — give every device its own strong, unique credential the moment you set it up.

items.lead: Buy from vendors who keep patching.
items.body: Prioritise companies with a proven record of security updates and transparent privacy policies, and know when a device's end-of-life arrives — the point its manufacturer stops issuing patches — so you can retire it before it becomes a liability.

closing.label: Minimising the Attack Surface
closing.lead: Every device you add to your network is a door — the fewer left unlocked, the smaller the target.
closing.body: Segmentation, unique credentials and knowing a device's end-of-life aren't extra precautions — they're what keeps the smart home's convenience from becoming its liability.

note: A doorbell camera goes up on a Saturday afternoon, paired to the app in minutes, admin password left exactly as it arrived from the factory. A thermostat follows a month later. Then a speaker, a plug socket, a baby monitor — each one landing on the same network as the laptop that holds the banking login, none of them getting the scrutiny that laptop would.
Every one of those devices is a door. Most homes now have more of them than the people living there could actually list, and almost none are ever checked for who's still allowed to walk through.

The card sets out three practices for a home full of connected devices — putting them on their own network, replacing the password they arrived with, and knowing a device's end-of-life before its manufacturer stops patching it. It's for anyone who's added a smart device to their network this year and not thought about it since.

It comes from The Shadow System, where the fuller argument about personal cybersecurity, and the systems built to exploit exactly this kind of inattention, gets made at length. The card doesn't need the book to make sense — it stands on its own.
Print it, or hand it to whoever in the house set up the last smart device without changing the password.
How many devices on your network right now could you actually name?

shape-your-networked-self.title: Shape Your Networked Self
shape-your-networked-self.line: For when the version of you online no longer feels like a decision you made.
shape-your-networked-self.subtitle: The version of you that exists across platforms and communities needs its own deliberate shape, not whatever each network defaults to.
shape-your-networked-self.quote: The greatest technology of all is still us.

items.lead: Notice how each platform makes you feel, not just what it shows you.
items.body: Pay attention to the interactions that shift your mood or self-perception, and name the content or exchanges that reliably trigger inadequacy or pressure to conform.

items.lead: Check your online persona against who you actually are.
items.body: Regularly ask whether your digital presence still lines up with your core values and the person you're trying to be offline.

items.lead: Decide what you share before a platform decides it for you.
items.body: Curate with purpose rather than letting a feed's defaults set your online identity, and segment which facets of yourself belong on which network.

items.lead: Take real breaks from your digital self.
items.body: Schedule regular disconnection so your offline self, your physical surroundings and your real-world relationships get their own uninterrupted time.

items.lead: Name your values before a platform names them for you.
items.body: Articulate what actually gives your life meaning, independent of likes, followers or any other digital metric.

items.lead: Spend real time on things a screen can't measure.
items.body: Invest deliberately in offline hobbies and relationships that build genuine connection and a sense of accomplishment no algorithm can touch.

groups.heading: Protect Your Digital Boundaries and Well-being

items.lead: Set limits before the platform sets them for you.
items.body: Establish clear boundaries on screen time and engagement, and be ruthless about unfollowing or muting anything that damages your self-esteem.

items.lead: Treat your privacy settings as an active decision, not a default.
items.body: Understand what each platform actually shares, and stay alert to what oversharing costs your personal and professional identity later.

items.lead: Invest first in the people in the room.
items.body: Prioritise face-to-face conversation and shared experience with family and friends over anything a screen can offer instead.

items.lead: Let technology open real relationships, not replace them.
items.body: Use online tools to bridge toward offline connection, and turn genuine online acquaintances into people you actually meet.

note: Alex has four different names for four different rooms — one on LinkedIn, one on a gaming server, one under an old university nickname nobody uses any more, and one that's just a photo and a bio nobody wrote carefully. None of them are lies, exactly. Each one just answers to a different audience, a different algorithm, a different version of what seemed safe to say at the time.

Coherence isn't the same as sameness. But somewhere between the tenth platform and the thirtieth persona, most people stop choosing who they are online and start absorbing whatever each network defaults to. The platforms didn't ask for permission to shape that. Nobody had to grant it — the shaping just happened, one default setting and one algorithmic nudge at a time, until the version of Alex that shows up somewhere wasn't really a decision at all.

The card sets out five practice areas, from noticing what a platform's mood-shifts are actually telling you to rebuilding the real-world relationships technology was only ever meant to support. It's written for anyone who's stopped noticing how many versions of themselves they're currently running.
It comes from The Next Evolution, where the fuller argument about identity, technology and coherence gets made at length. The card doesn't need the book to make sense — it stands on its own.
Print it, or send it to whoever's about to open their fifth tab of the day without noticing they did.
If nobody built your online self on purpose, who actually did?

the-digital-sieve.title: The Digital Sieve
the-digital-sieve.line: For when you realise the version of the world you're reacting to was assembled before you ever looked at it.
the-digital-sieve.subtitle: Most of what reaches you was already filtered before you saw it. This pause hands that filtering back to you.
the-digital-sieve.quote: The future will be shaped by what we choose to attend to.

items.lead: Notice what actually sends you reaching for your phone.
items.body: Boredom, a notification, a moment of stress — name the trigger and you can start to interrupt it, rather than acting on it automatically.

items.lead: Name the reward you're actually chasing — a like, new content, a message.
items.body: Ask honestly whether it lines up with what you want from your time, or just with what keeps you opening the app.

items.lead: Put a small obstacle between yourself and the compulsive reach.
items.body: Remove the app from your home screen, log out after each use, turn off the notification — friction a habit has to work around.

items.lead: Swap the digital habit for an offline one the moment the urge arrives.
items.body: Choose something that actually serves you, not just whatever isn't a screen.

items.lead: Tell the people close to you what you've learned about the Hook Model and addictive design.
items.body: Shared awareness makes healthier habits easier to keep, for you and for them.

items.lead: Studies how cues, routines and rewards drive human behaviour.
items.body: Particularly revealing once you apply it to a habit that plays out entirely on a screen.

items.lead: Studies how design choices are used deliberately to shape what you do next.
items.body: The interface in front of you was built by someone whose job was influencing your behaviour, not just making the product usable.

items.lead: Studies the clinical and psychological impact of problematic internet and phone use.
items.body: Where habit tips into compulsion, and what the evidence says actually helps.

items.lead: Studies how game mechanics get applied outside games to drive engagement.
items.body: Points, streaks and levels didn't arrive in your apps by accident — they arrived because they work.

items.lead: Studies the brain's dopamine pathways and their role in seeking behaviour.
items.body: The chemistry behind the reach explains why willpower alone rarely beats a well-designed reward loop.

closing.lead: This isn't about achieving flawless scepticism.
closing.body: It's about becoming an active filter rather than a passive receiver — someone who chooses deliberately what to accept, question and discard, so what shapes your view of the world is actually yours.

note: Open your phone at any moment today and something is already waiting — a headline, a notification, a video queued up next. None of it arrived by accident. Somewhere between the event and your screen, a sieve decided what got through and what didn't, and it wasn't you holding it.

That sieve doesn't just filter information. It reinforces whatever you already lean toward, narrows the range of what you actually see, and hands you the result as your view of the world. This pause asks the simpler question underneath: who's doing the filtering, and how much of that job can you take back?

The card lays out ten things to explore, in two columns. Try Something is five habits for noticing your own patterns before reacting to them — naming what triggers the reach for a phone, auditing the reward a platform is actually giving you, building friction into a habit that currently has none. Learn Something is five fields worth a longer look, from the behavioural economics of habit formation to the neuroscience of the reward systems those habits run on.

It comes from The Cognitive Crucible, where the fuller argument about the Digital Sieve and the Cognitive Crucible it feeds gets made at length. The card doesn't need the book to make sense — it stands on its own.
Print it, pin it somewhere you'll actually see it, or send it to whoever in your life has stopped asking where their feed comes from.
The card doesn't resolve the harder part: once you can name the sieve, how much of what's already settled in your head are you willing to go back and re-examine?

navigate-the-geopolitics-of-technology-a.title: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
navigate-the-geopolitics-of-technology-a.line: For when a technical standard turns out to be a foreign policy decision nobody voted on.
navigate-the-geopolitics-of-technology-a.subtitle: Digital infrastructure now shapes global power as much as any treaty does, and governance keeps arriving after the decisions that matter are already made.
navigate-the-geopolitics-of-technology-a.quote: The greatest technology of all is still us.

items.lead: Build dedicated channels for technology diplomacy.
items.body: Formal and informal forums that bring governments, companies, civil society and academia together work through a technology's impact before deployment, not after.

items.lead: Find shared definitions before you need them.
items.body: Common understandings of ethical AI, data governance and cybersecurity norms across different political and cultural contexts make later disagreement something you can actually resolve.

items.lead: Resist the fragmentation of the internet.
items.body: Open, interoperable standards keep systems connected across borders; a balkanised internet just hands each fragment to whoever controls it.

items.lead: Diversify the supply chains that hold everything up.
items.body: Work multilaterally to reduce single points of failure in critical technology supply chains, without retreating into protectionism to do it.

items.lead: Design regulation that can move as fast as the technology.
items.body: Iterative, flexible agreements outlast rules written for a specific technology that will be obsolete before they're ratified.

items.lead: Regulate outcomes, not technologies.
items.body: A focus on impact rather than mechanism gives bodies like the UN, ITU and WTO the mandate to keep pace as new technologies arrive, rather than rewriting the rulebook each time.

groups.heading: Prioritise Human Rights and Ethical Considerations Globally

items.lead: Hold human rights standards above sovereignty claims.
items.body: Privacy, freedom of expression and non-discrimination shouldn't bend to whichever jurisdiction happens to be enforcing them.

items.lead: Push for ethical AI treaties with actual teeth.
items.body: International agreements on autonomous weapons, surveillance and algorithmic bias matter more, not less, once the technological capacity to act on them is already there.

closing.label: What's Actually at Stake
closing.lead: The rules for this technology are being written right now, by whoever shows up.
closing.body: Waiting for governance to catch up isn't neutral — it's a decision to let someone else's interests fill the gap.

note: A single company sets the protocol that every connected device in a region ends up speaking, and a government three time zones away finds its infrastructure now depends on a standard it had no hand in writing. Nobody signed a treaty. There was no vote. The standard simply won, because it shipped first and governance hadn't caught up yet.

That pattern repeats across chips, cloud contracts, undersea cables and the training data behind the models a country's own services now run on. Technology has stopped being just a tool nations use and become a form of power they compete over — and the rules meant to govern that competition are still being drafted while the competition is already well under way.

The card holds four practice areas in one column: fostering real technology diplomacy between governments, companies and civil society; championing open standards against the pull toward a fragmented internet; building governance frameworks flexible enough to survive contact with a fast-moving technology; and holding human rights above whichever jurisdiction's convenience is being served. Written for anyone who wants to see the politics inside the technology, not just the engineering.
It comes from The Next Evolution, where the fuller argument lives. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, or send it to whoever keeps saying this is a technical decision, not a political one.
If the standard is already decided by the time governance arrives, who was actually in the room?

reclaiming-your-inner-landscape.title: Reclaiming Your Inner Landscape
reclaiming-your-inner-landscape.line: For when the fog by mid-afternoon has started to feel less like a mood and more like a fact of the day.
reclaiming-your-inner-landscape.subtitle: The attention economy doesn't just cost you time — it costs you the mind you come home to. This pause is about taking it back.
reclaiming-your-inner-landscape.quote: The future will be shaped by what we choose to attend to.

items.lead: Set clear times for disconnecting from work email and social media.
items.body: Use 'do not disturb' modes to make the boundary automatic rather than something you have to enforce by willpower alone.

items.lead: Schedule dedicated blocks of uninterrupted time for complex tasks.
items.body: Free the block from digital distractions entirely — deep work and partial attention can't coexist in the same window.

items.lead: Take short breaks or longer periods away from screens on a regular basis.
items.body: The reset isn't about willpower during the break — it's about what resuming with a clearer mind lets you notice afterwards.

items.lead: Engage in activities that don't involve a screen at all.
items.body: A different kind of engagement — one that doesn't compete for the same attention a feed is built to hold.

items.lead: Pay attention to how different digital interactions actually make you feel.
items.body: If a platform consistently leaves you anxious or inadequate, that's information worth acting on, not ignoring.

items.lead: Build a consistent bedtime routine, screens off for at least an hour before sleep.
items.body: The last hour of the day is also the hour most vulnerable to a feed with nothing better to do than hold you there.

items.lead: Studies the links between technology use and conditions like anxiety, depression and loneliness.
items.body: The correlations are well documented; the harder question is which uses cause harm and which merely track it.

items.lead: Studies how information overload and multitasking affect cognitive performance and decision-making.
items.body: Every open tab and notification is a small tax on the working memory you need for the task in front of you.

items.lead: Researches the brain mechanisms behind sustained attention, distraction and mental exhaustion.
items.body: Attention is a finite resource with a biological cost — fatigue isn't a character flaw, it's a measurable limit.

items.lead: Studies which strategies for reducing screen time actually work, and which only feel like they do.
items.body: The evidence base for most popular interventions is thinner than the wellness industry suggests.

items.lead: Studies how technology and the attention economy are reshaping work patterns and personal boundaries.
items.body: The boundary between work and rest didn't erode by accident — the always-on expectation was built into the tools.

closing.lead: The goal isn't to reject the digital world you live in.
closing.body: It's to move from captive participant to intentional steward of your own mind and time — building a life shaped by your values rather than whatever's engineered to hold your attention next.

note: You reach for your phone before you've decided to. Somewhere between waking and actually being awake, the scroll has already started, and by the time you notice, an hour of the day has gone somewhere you didn't choose to send it.

That fog has a cause, not just a name. The attention economy isn't a metaphor — it's a system built to hold you longer than you meant to stay, and the fatigue, the fractured focus, the thinning stretch of face-to-face time are its actual output, not a side effect you can shrug off.

The card splits into two columns — six things to try, from digital boundaries to sleep hygiene, and five research threads for anyone who wants to go further, from cognitive load theory to the neuroscience of attention and fatigue. It's for anyone who's noticed the fog and wants a way back out of it.
It comes from The Cognitive Crucible, where the fuller argument about attention, technology and the mind lives. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, pin it somewhere you'll see it before you next reach for your phone, or send it to someone who's been meaning to make this change.
What would you actually notice, if you paid attention to how a day online makes you feel?

reclaim-your-engagement.title: Reclaim Your Engagement
reclaim-your-engagement.line: For when you look up and can't remember choosing to scroll this far.
reclaim-your-engagement.subtitle: Every swipe and pause is measured and monetised by systems built to hold you, not inform you — reclaiming it starts with seeing the architecture.
reclaim-your-engagement.quote: The greatest technology of all is still us.

items.lead: Learn to spot the design patterns built to hook you.
items.body: Infinite scroll, streaks, notifications and fear of missing out are engineered, not accidental — name them when you see them.

items.lead: Audit where your attention actually goes.
items.body: Use screen time reports or your own journal to compare real usage against what you intended, and remember a 'free' product is usually paid for with your attention.

items.lead: Turn off what's designed to pull you back in.
items.body: Disable non-essential notifications, autoplay and personalised recommendations, and use ad blockers or focus tools to blunt algorithmic influence.

items.lead: Build routines for how and when you engage.
items.body: Curate your feeds ruthlessly, and design specific windows for checking platforms rather than letting them interrupt you at will.

items.lead: Protect blocks of time a notification can't reach.
items.body: Dedicate uninterrupted stretches to deep work, creative pursuits or offline conversation, and defend them from digital intrusion.

items.lead: Choose participation over consumption.
items.body: Favour creating, discussing and learning over passive scrolling, and seek out slower spaces that reward thoughtful discussion over rapid-fire engagement.

items.lead: Audit your own product for manipulation, not just usability.
items.body: Regularly assess features for manipulative patterns and their real impact on a user's mental health, time and agency.

items.lead: Measure value created, not just time spent.
items.body: Give users clear, robust controls over notifications, algorithms and usage limits, and shift your own metrics toward genuine value and wellbeing.

groups.heading: Foster a Transparent & Fair Data Economy

items.lead: Say plainly what data you collect and why it benefits the user.
items.body: Replace opaque terms and conditions with a clear value exchange, and experiment with business models that don't depend solely on advertising or extraction.

items.lead: Champion the user's right to their own data.
items.body: Support policies and technologies that give people real ownership and control over their personal data, including the right to decide how it's used.

items.lead: Teach users how the attention economy actually works.
items.body: Build features and prompts that grow digital literacy and critical thinking directly into the product, not as a separate education campaign.

items.lead: Lead internally the way you ask users to behave.
items.body: Make user wellbeing and ethical practice part of your own culture and product development, not just your public messaging.

note: Jordan opens the phone to check one thing. Twenty minutes disappear before the original question even gets answered. Nothing about those twenty minutes was accidental — the interface, the notification, the infinite feed, all of it was built by people who understood exactly which nudge would keep a thumb moving.

Attention isn't just spent there. It's shaped there — what you focus on for that long starts shaping what you believe matters, whether you meant it to or not. The apps calling themselves free were never really free. Somebody paid for the engineering that made twenty minutes disappear, and the payment came out of exactly the resource that just vanished.

The card splits into two columns — three practices for anyone trying to take their attention back, and three for the platform builders and product leaders deciding what gets built in the first place. It's for the person on either side of that design decision.

It comes from The Next Evolution, where the fuller argument about attention, engagement and the systems built to hold it gets made at length. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, or send it to whoever just told you they don't have time to read any more.
If the platform is optimising for your attention, what exactly are you optimising for?

the-historical-roots-of-persuasion.title: The Historical Roots of Persuasion
the-historical-roots-of-persuasion.line: For when the ad you just watched felt like it knew you a little too well.
the-historical-roots-of-persuasion.subtitle: The tactics working on you today aren't new — they have a history, and it's worth knowing whose interest it was built to serve.
the-historical-roots-of-persuasion.quote: The future will be shaped by what we choose to attend to.

items.lead: Notice the psychological tactics at work in the ads you actually encounter.
items.body: Emotional appeals, scarcity, authority — the techniques repeat once you know to look for them, across TV, print and online.

items.lead: Pause before a purchase and ask whether you need it, or whether the desire was manufactured.
items.body: Marketing's job is to make a want feel like a need — the pause is what tells the two apart.

items.lead: Look into how major brands built their identity and captured loyalty over time.
items.body: The playbook is decades old; seeing its origins makes today's version easier to recognise.

items.lead: Talk to older generations about how advertising has changed over their lifetime.
items.body: Their memory of what persuasion used to look like is a useful baseline for measuring what it's become.

items.lead: Watch for when an idea is being engineered into public discourse rather than arrived at.
items.body: Public relations works best when it's invisible — spotting the campaign is the first step to weighing it fairly.

items.lead: Studies how advertising techniques and agencies developed, and their impact on consumer culture.
items.body: The industry that shapes today's attention economy has a documented history — none of this started with the internet.

items.lead: Researches the origins of PR, including figures like Edward Bernays and their influence on public opinion.
items.body: Modern persuasion techniques were formalised nearly a century ago, often explicitly modelled on propaganda.

items.lead: Studies early experiments and theories on consumer behaviour, motivation and decision-making.
items.body: Much of what platforms use today was tested on shoppers long before it was tested on scrollers.

items.lead: Traces the historical development of branding strategies and their role in market competition.
items.body: A brand is a persuasion structure built to outlast any single campaign — understanding it changes how loyalty reads.

items.lead: Studies how industrialisation and mass production gave rise to consumer societies.
items.body: Attention became a commodity long before data did — the commodification of information and attention is the same story continued.

closing.lead: Your attention has always been a resource with a cost.
closing.body: Recognising the exchange — rather than accepting it as invisible — is what moves you from product to a discerning participant in it.

note: An advert doesn't need to be clever to work. It needs a want that feels like a need, a moment of urgency, a face you're inclined to trust. None of that is new — the platform delivering it is the only part of the equation that's actually changed.

Edward Bernays was formalising public opinion into a discipline a century before anyone had a feed to scroll. The techniques working on you now have a lineage, built by people who understood exactly what they were doing, long before data made the targeting precise.

The card splits into two columns — five things to try, from analysing the ads in front of you to tracing a brand's own history, and five research threads for anyone who wants the fuller picture, from the history of advertising to the economic rise of consumer societies. It's for anyone who wants to see the architecture behind the message, not just the message.
It comes from The Cognitive Crucible, where the fuller argument about attention, technology and persuasion lives. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, pin it somewhere you'll actually see it, or send it to someone who still thinks this started with the internet.
If persuasion has always had a history, whose interest was it actually built to serve?

fortify-the-enterprise.title: Fortify the Enterprise
fortify-the-enterprise.line: For when the human element is your strongest layer of defence, not your weakest.
fortify-the-enterprise.subtitle: Corporate resilience is not a technology purchase — it's people, process and partners working from the same playbook.
fortify-the-enterprise.quote: Resilience isn't measured by the absence of incidents.

items.lead: Train for the scenario, not the slogan.
items.body: Move beyond generic awareness videos — regular, scenario-based sessions teach employees to spot mismatched URLs, false urgency and unusual tone before they click.

items.lead: Treat failure as a teaching moment.
items.body: Run routine phishing simulations and use the outcomes to educate, not discipline — punishing a click teaches people to hide it, not to avoid it next time.

items.lead: Build a blame-free reporting culture.
items.body: Make 'see something, say something' real: every suspicious link reported early is a breach prevented, and speaking up should never carry a cost.

items.lead: Build the response team before the breach.
items.body: IT, legal, communications, operations and HR each have a role in a crisis — nobody should be learning theirs when the alarm sounds.

items.lead: Decide who speaks, before anyone needs to.
items.body: Prepare transparent, pre-approved statements for employees, customers, regulators and media so a crisis doesn't also become a communications failure.

items.lead: Rehearse the whole lifecycle.
items.body: Detection, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident review — test the plan with tabletop exercises and live simulations, because an untested plan is an unproven one.

items.lead: Verify before you onboard.
items.body: Require documentation of a vendor's security maturity — certifications, policies and incident response protocols — before granting them access to your systems.

items.lead: Make resilience a contractual obligation.
items.body: Specify encryption, breach notification and continuous vulnerability assessment in every vendor contract; don't leave security as an assumption.

items.lead: Grant access on need, not convenience.
items.body: Review vendor permissions regularly and revoke credentials the moment they're no longer required — a forgotten login is an open door.

closing.label: From Compliance to Continuity
closing.lead: Resilience isn't a compliance checkbox — it's a competitive advantage.
closing.body: The most secure enterprises don't chase every new threat; they build adaptable systems, nurture vigilance, and plan for recovery before the crisis hits. Security signals governance maturity, and in markets where trust determines longevity, that maturity is the differentiator.

note: A finance assistant gets an email from someone who signs off exactly like the CFO always does. The tone is right. The urgency is right. The only thing wrong is that the CFO didn't send it. Somewhere in a training video months earlier, someone told this assistant to be careful — but caution isn't what saves the transfer. Recognition is.

Most companies still treat security as an IT department problem with a compliance layer bolted on. The organisations that actually survive an attack treat it differently: as a discipline that runs through every desk, every vendor contract, every crisis rehearsal, long before anything goes wrong.

The card sets out three practice areas. The human element trains people to recognise manipulation, not just avoid it. The tactical core builds and tests an incident response plan before it's needed, not during the breach. The extended perimeter holds suppliers and vendors to the same standard as the business itself. It's written for leaders and the teams they run, not just IT.

It comes from The Shadow System, the closing book of the trilogy, where the fuller argument about organisational resilience gets made at length. The card doesn't need the book to make sense — it stands on its own.
Print it for the team that owns your incident response plan, or send it to the leader who still thinks a firewall is where the job ends.
Every practice area on this card assumes a breach will eventually reach you. The harder question it leaves open: does your organisation actually rehearse for that day, or just insure against it?

engage-with-human-augmentation-for-cogni.title: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
engage-with-human-augmentation-for-cogni.line: For when the tool meant to sharpen your thinking starts doing some of the thinking for you.
engage-with-human-augmentation-for-cogni.subtitle: Neural interfaces, cognitive prosthetics and AI companions are already extending memory, focus and judgement — the question is what they're extending it toward.
engage-with-human-augmentation-for-cogni.quote: The greatest technology of all is still us.

items.lead: Name the specific thing you're trying to improve.
items.body: Memory, focus, learning speed, sensory perception — a vague ambition to be "more enhanced" leads to tools adopted for their own sake, not for what they're actually for.

items.lead: Weigh the ethics before you weigh the benefit.
items.body: Ask whether the augmentation is safe and equitable, and whether it aligns with your own values, before asking whether it works.

items.lead: Separate the evidenced from the speculative.
items.body: Smart wearables, brain-computer interfaces, nootropics and AI-driven learning tools sit at very different points on the evidence spectrum — know which one you're actually being offered.

items.lead: Check what it does with your cognitive data before you check what it does for you.
items.body: A tool that reads focus, memory or attention is also collecting some of the most personal data there is. Prioritise the ones with real privacy protection built in.

items.lead: Start with the lowest-impact option available.
items.body: Smart notepads and focus apps before brain-computer interfaces. Augmentation is a skill to be learned, not a switch to be flipped.

items.lead: Keep the fundamentals in place underneath it.
items.body: Sleep, nutrition, exercise and stress management don't get replaced by a tool that complements them — monitor whether the augmentation is actually adding to those foundations or quietly eroding them.

groups.heading: Maintain a Balanced and Ethical Perspective

items.lead: Keep your unaugmented thinking in working order.
items.body: Over-reliance risks diminishing the very capacity the tool was meant to support — notice if you're becoming more efficient at tasks while becoming less capable without the tool.

items.lead: Advocate for access, not just adoption.
items.body: Beneficial augmentation technologies won't reach everyone by default. Push for policies that make fair access to them part of the plan, not an afterthought.

closing.label: What This Actually Asks of You
closing.lead: Augmentation amplifies whatever intention you bring to it.
closing.body: Clarity about what you're enhancing, and why, is the difference between a tool that deepens your judgement and one that quietly replaces it.

note: A focus app promises fewer distractions and delivers them, at first — until the habit of checking whether you're focused becomes its own distraction. A nootropic promises clearer thinking. A brain-computer interface, still mostly experimental, promises something closer to a new sense. Each one is real. None of them arrives with a label explaining what it's quietly asking you to give up in exchange.

Cognitive enhancement is no longer a thought experiment. Neural interfaces, wearables and AI companions already extend memory, focus and decision-making for people using them today, and the tools are getting less experimental by the year. What's missing isn't the technology — it's the discipline of asking what a given augmentation actually does to the person using it, before adopting it because it's available.

The card holds four practice areas in one column: assessing your own needs and goals before reaching for a tool, evaluating augmentation technologies on evidence rather than hype, implementing them thoughtfully starting with the lowest-impact option, and maintaining a balanced, ethical perspective on what the tool is actually doing to your own capacities. Written for anyone experimenting with these tools now, not waiting for a future version of them.
It comes from The Next Evolution, where the fuller argument lives. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, or send it to whoever just downloaded a focus app without asking what it's tracking.
If a tool makes you more efficient and less capable without it, has it enhanced you, or replaced part of you?

asserting-your-digital-self.title: Asserting Your Digital Self
asserting-your-digital-self.line: For when the profile you built stopped looking like you.
asserting-your-digital-self.subtitle: Your online profile was built to hold the platform's attention, not necessarily to be you. This pause is about closing that gap on purpose.
asserting-your-digital-self.quote: The future will be shaped by what we choose to attend to.

items.lead: Review your online accounts and delete the ones you no longer use.
items.body: For everything that stays active, strengthen the password and turn on multi-factor authentication — an old account nobody remembers is still a door nobody's watching.

items.lead: Turn on two-factor authentication for email, banking and social media.
items.body: These are the accounts that unlock everything else — a second factor here is the strongest single lock available to you.

items.lead: Find out how your biometric data is actually stored before you hand over a fingerprint or a face scan.
items.body: Unlike a password, a compromised fingerprint can't be reset — know what you're trusting a device or service to protect.

items.lead: Try a VPN, a privacy-focused browser or a secure messaging app for a week.
items.body: See what the difference actually feels like before deciding whether it's worth keeping.

items.lead: Decide what should happen to your accounts and data after you're gone.
items.body: Most platforms have a legacy or memorialisation setting — the choice sits with you until you make it, then it defaults to whatever the platform decides.

items.lead: Studies new authentication methods and the defences against identity theft and account takeover.
items.body: The tools protecting your accounts are changing faster than most people update their passwords.

items.lead: Studies how privacy gets built into a system from the start, rather than added afterwards.
items.body: Privacy by design shapes what a product can do with your data before you ever click accept.

items.lead: Explores blockchain-based and other decentralised approaches to managing identity.
items.body: The aim is an identity you hold and control directly, rather than one issued and verified by a single company.

items.lead: Studies how to design security that people will actually use correctly.
items.body: The strongest protection in theory is worth little if it's too awkward for anyone to keep using it.

items.lead: Investigates how digital identity crimes happen and how they get prevented.
items.body: Understanding how identity theft is actually carried out is the fastest way to see where your own exposure sits.

closing.lead: This isn't about performing a perfect persona.
closing.body: It's about becoming the conscious author of your own identity — closing the distance between who you are and who you present yourself to be, so your digital identity reflects you rather than an algorithm's incentives.

note: Scroll back through an old account — a profile on a platform you barely open anymore — and the person looking back can feel like a stranger. The photos are chosen, the bio is polished, the opinions performed for an audience that mostly isn't there anymore. None of that happened by accident.

Every platform nudges you toward a version of yourself that serves its own numbers: more time in the app, more content shared, more data handed over. The incentive sits with the platform, not with you — a profile engineered to hold attention is doing exactly what it was built to do. Left unattended, the gap between that curated self and the person living the rest of your life grows quietly, until closing it starts to feel like the harder task.

The card splits into two columns — five actions to try this week, from auditing old accounts to deciding what happens to your data when you're gone, and five research threads for anyone who wants to go further, from privacy engineering to decentralised identity systems. It's built for anyone whose online self has started to feel like someone else's project, not just the security-conscious.
It comes from The Cognitive Crucible, where the fuller argument about identity, algorithms and self-authorship lives. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, pin it near your desk, or send it to whoever just deleted an old account and felt strangely relieved.
Which version of you would a stranger meet first — the one online, or the one in the room?

defend-your-identity-from-theft-and-impe.title: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
defend-your-identity-from-theft-and-impe.line: For when the voice on the phone sounds exactly like someone you trust.
defend-your-identity-from-theft-and-impe.subtitle: Deepfakes, identity spoofing and AI-generated personas are no longer science fiction — they're operational risks to who you're taken to be.
defend-your-identity-from-theft-and-impe.quote: The greatest technology of all is still us.

items.lead: Move past passwords and static biometrics alone.
items.body: Build multi-modal, context-aware identity systems that weigh behavioural cues and provenance chains, not just a single credential.

items.lead: Put a legal penalty on malicious digital cloning.
items.body: Create legislation that defines and penalises the deliberate creation or use of deepfakes, voice simulations and digital clones.

items.lead: Make synthetic media identifiable by default.
items.body: Encourage watermarking of AI-generated content and maintain public registries of official synthetic personas.

items.lead: Give investigators more than forensic computing skills.
items.body: Blend forensic computing with psychological analysis, narrative detection and deep learning literacy.

groups.heading: Keep a Human in High-Stakes Decisions

items.lead: Never let identity determinations run fully automated.
items.body: Ensure human oversight in systems making high-stakes identity decisions, especially in immigration, welfare or justice.

items.lead: Be cautious with your biometric, visual and voice data.
items.body: Once uploaded, any of it can be replicated — think before you share your face, your voice or your fingerprints online.

items.lead: Treat convincing content with a healthy question first.
items.body: Ask whether what you're seeing could be synthetic, and use tools or plug-ins built to verify authenticity.

groups.heading: Claim Your Likeness as Your Property

items.lead: Advocate for legal ownership over your own digital likeness.
items.body: Push for laws that treat it as your intellectual property, giving you the right to license or block its use.

items.lead: Choose products that are honest about synthetic media.
items.body: Promote platforms that disclose their use of synthetic media and uphold anti-impersonation safeguards.

groups.heading: Spread the Skills to Spot Manipulation

items.lead: Equip the people around you to recognise manipulated content.
items.body: Focus especially on the very young and the elderly, and support reporting manipulated content when you see it.

note: A grandparent gets a call. The voice is unmistakable — a grandchild, panicked, in trouble, needing money sent immediately. Every inflection is right. None of it is real. Three seconds of audio pulled from a video online was enough to build a voice that could ask for anything and be believed.

Identity used to be something you protected by keeping a password secret. Now it's something that can be manufactured, in seconds, from material you never agreed to give away — a video posted years ago, a voicemail greeting, a face captured in someone else's photo. None of it required your consent to become raw material.

The card sets out five practice areas for policymakers and law enforcement, and five for citizens and civil society — from redesigning identity frameworks that still rely on a single static credential, to knowing when to simply ask whether what you're looking at is real. It's for anyone who assumed impersonation still took real effort.
It comes from The Next Evolution, where the fuller argument about identity, trust and emerging cybercrime gets made at length. The card doesn't need the book to make sense — it stands on its own.
Print it, or send it to the relative most likely to answer an urgent call without checking first.
If a voice can be manufactured this convincingly, what's left that actually proves it's you?

designing-your-digital-life.title: Designing Your Digital Life
designing-your-digital-life.line: For when the apps you didn't choose start choosing for you.
designing-your-digital-life.subtitle: Every app you use reflects a choice someone else made about your attention. This pause is about making a few choices of your own.
designing-your-digital-life.quote: The future will be shaped by what we choose to attend to.

items.lead: Look for apps and services that put your well-being first, with granular controls and transparent data practices.
items.body: A product built around your attention and one built around your well-being rarely look the same once you check the settings.

items.lead: Choose subscription-based services over ad-supported ones where you can.
items.body: Aligning the product's incentive with your interest, not the advertiser's, changes what it's actually built to want from you.

items.lead: Tell tech companies directly when a feature helps your well-being, and when it just distracts you.
items.body: Companies respond to what users tell them matters — silence reads as consent.

items.lead: Share what you know about ethical design and humane technology with the people around you.
items.body: Awareness spreads the same way distraction does — one person at a time.

items.lead: Ask yourself before opening an app: am I using this tool, or is it using me?
items.body: The honest answer changes depending on the app, and on the day — that's exactly why it's worth asking.

items.lead: Studies how to design technology that prioritises human needs, values and well-being.
items.body: Good intentions in a design brief mean little without the practice to back them up.

groups.heading: Digital Ethics and Philosophy of Technology

items.lead: Explores the moral questions behind technology design, data collection and algorithmic influence.
items.body: The technical choices in a product are ethical ones too, whether or not anyone treats them that way.

items.lead: Explores revenue models that don't rely on capturing attention or exploiting data.
items.body: A business that doesn't need your attention to survive changes what the product is built to want from you.

items.lead: Studies whether design features and apps aimed at healthier tech habits actually work.
items.body: Plenty of apps promise better habits — the evidence on which ones deliver is thinner than the marketing.

items.lead: Studies how to make algorithms more understandable, fair and auditable.
items.body: An algorithm you can't inspect is a decision you're asked to trust without ever seeing the reasoning.

closing.lead: This isn't about rejecting every tool that asks for your attention.
closing.body: It's about developing a critical eye for the intention behind the interfaces you use, so you choose technology that serves your values rather than defaulting into whatever the platform hands you.

note: Open any app you didn't design and you're using someone else's decisions — what the button says, where it sits, how many taps stand between you and closing the thing. None of it is neutral. Every choice was made by a person answering to a target that has nothing to do with your evening.
Most of the time that stays invisible. It only surfaces in a small moment — reaching for the phone and catching yourself mid-reach, wondering who actually decided you'd do that.

The card splits into two columns — five things to try this week, from seeking out subscription models that don't need your attention to asking one honest question before opening an app, and five research threads for anyone who wants to go further, from human-centred design to algorithmic accountability. It's for anyone who's noticed the gap between what an app claims to offer and what it's actually built to extract.
It comes from The Cognitive Crucible, where the fuller argument about attention, design and human agency lives. The card stands on its own — you don't need the book to use it.
Print it, pin it by your desk, or send it to whoever just deleted an app and felt lighter for it.
Which of your daily apps would survive being redesigned around your interest instead of theirs?

cultivate-conscious-perception-in-virtua.title: Cultivate Conscious Perception in Virtual Frontiers
cultivate-conscious-perception-in-virtua.line: For when an environment reaches your senses before it reaches your judgement.
cultivate-conscious-perception-in-virtua.subtitle: Staying present, embodied and in control of your own senses as immersive environments become sensory, emotional and designed to surround you.
cultivate-conscious-perception-in-virtua.quote: The greatest technology of all is still us.

items.lead: Learn to tell real sensory input from digitally mediated ones.
items.body: Develop a critical awareness of what's authentic in an environment and what's simulated.

items.lead: Question the intent behind sensory cues.
items.body: Haptic feedback, subtle scents and auditory cues can be designed to evoke specific emotional or behavioural responses.

items.lead: Run regular sensory audits.
items.body: Disconnect from immersive technology and re-engage with unmediated senses — nature, simple tastes, plain smells — to recalibrate your perception.

items.lead: Set clear time limits on immersive engagement.
items.body: Prevent over-stimulation, desensitisation or addiction before it starts.

items.lead: Be selective about what earns your full senses.
items.body: Prioritise experiences that offer genuine value, learning, creativity or meaningful connection.

items.lead: Know who is reading your physiological responses.
items.body: Biometric sensors can track how your body reacts to virtual stimuli — understand and control who has access to that intimate data.

items.lead: Seek out experiences that expand you.
items.body: Look for environments that grow your empathy, teach new skills, or open up collaborative creativity.

items.lead: Push developers to label manipulative content.
items.body: Advocate for clear flags on sensory-manipulative design, and real transparency in sensory data collection.

items.lead: Build collective understanding of the Internet of Senses.
items.body: Educate yourself and others on the psychological and physiological impacts of uncritical engagement.

items.lead: Run psychological impact assessments before launch.
items.body: Weigh the potential for addiction, desensitisation or mental health harm in any highly sensory experience.

items.lead: Give users granular control over sensory intensity.
items.body: Let people customise their own level of immersion and comfort.

items.lead: Build real off-ramps into every experience.
items.body: Design clear endings and decompression zones so users can disengage and reintegrate without disorientation or overload.

items.lead: Get clear, revocable consent for sensory data.
items.body: Eye-tracking, galvanic skin response and haptic feedback data all need informed permission, not assumed access.

items.lead: Explain how and why AI customises the experience.
items.body: Give users the ability to understand and adjust the parameters shaping what they feel.

items.lead: Hold biometric data to the highest security standard.
items.body: Anonymise and protect any sensitive sensory response data you collect.

items.lead: Put ethics ahead of technical capability.
items.body: This matters most with haptic, olfactory or gustatory interfaces that can directly shape perception and emotion.

items.lead: Build industry standards with your peers.
items.body: Work together on content ratings, data privacy and user safety for the Internet of Senses.

items.lead: Help the public understand what these systems do.
items.body: Support initiatives that explain the Internet of Senses, so people can engage with it critically and consciously.

note: A training simulation ends and the trainee lifts the headset off. For a few seconds the real room feels subtly wrong — the colours flat, the floor too still. That passes. What stays behind is the record the session made: where the eyes went, how long each gaze was held, and how the skin's electrical response shifted at the moment the scenario turned difficult.

Immersive environments have stopped being something you look at. They arrive through sight, sound, touch and, increasingly, scent, and they land in the body before any argument reaches the mind. That makes perception itself something a designer sets parameters for. It becomes possible to build an experience that genuinely grows a person's empathy — and equally possible to build one that holds them by keeping the nervous system occupied. The same toolkit does both, and from inside the headset the two feel identical.
